newsitem.title: UK: UK hard pushed to meet PSBR targets - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK hard pushed to meet PSBR targets - analysts.

text.p: Britain's budget on Tuesday gave a surprisingly optimistic outlook for the nation's public finances, one economists said Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would be hard pushed to deliver.
They said the forecasts relied too heavily on tough spending cuts and ill-defined tax raising plans.

"He's being quite optimistic and they are contingent on some of the toughest spending plans ever," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr. "I don't think they're going to be able to meet them."

Clarke revised down his forecast for the Public Sector Borrowing Requirement (PSBR) by 400 million sterling in 1996/97 to 26.5 billion stg and slashed his 1997/98 forecast by four billion stg to 19 billion. Analysts had been expecting a more modest revision of two billion sterling in 1997/98.
"What really worries me is the rather nebulous figures about how much is to be raised by clamping down on fraud and the black economy," said General Accident economist Andrew Milligan.
Clarke said a crackdown on "some of the clever wheezes" he said had sprung up to avoid Value Added Tax (VAT) would raise 750 million stg next year.
He added a spend-to-save package of tax avoidance measures costing 800 million sterling over the next three years would secure revenue and expenditure savings of 6.7 billion sterling.
HSBC markets economist Jonathan Loynes was slightly less pessimistic about the chances of reaching the new PSBR target, citing what appeared to be strong tax receipts.
"I don't see why 19 billion sterling can't be achieved," he said.
"The latest figures suggest tax reciepts may be coming in rather more strongly than now. Along with the cuts in the control total, I think that is a reasonable PSBR forecast."
Clarke said the UK's PSBR would be broadly in balance by 1999-2000, a forecast greeted by analysts with some scepticism.
"The PSBR forecasts were realistic because of the upward growth revision," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at BT Gilts. "Maybe balancing the budget by 2000 is a little bit optimistic."
Clarke added the UK would meet Maastricht convergence criteria on debt and the public sector deficit in 1997 and would better them in the medium term.
"It'll be nice for Clarke to be able to say in Europe we'll meet the Maastricht criteria, even though it doesn't mean much domestically," Barr said.
Analysts said the Chancellor was prudent to revise his 1996/97 target only marginally.
"He very wisely decided not to lower the forecast for this year too much because he's not sure if the good (PSDR) figure in October will be repeated in January," said Milligan.
A net repayment of 4.4 billion sterling was made into government coffers in October, largely thanks to buoyant corporate tax receipts.
